cim: Stroke: how much does DNA really influence the risk? Artificial Intelligence will tell us
cim_eredeti: Stroke: how much does DNA really influence the risk? Artificial Intelligence will tell us

The figures speak for themselves. They show that around 10–15 per cent of all strokes occur in people under 50, with a higher prevalence among young women. Above all, in terms of trends, studies are confirming that ischaemic stroke in young adults is on the rise due to increased exposure to classic risk factors such as high blood pressure, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, smoking and being overweight. But the more research progresses, the more important it becomes to understand that we need to look beyond these factors – including the impact of alcohol and illicit drugs – to grasp the extent to which, and the ways in which, genetic predisposition plays a role, by combining an individual’s DNA information with lifestyle factors and other variables. Artificial Intelligence is needed to bring all these elements together.

And it is precisely an AI model tailored to this issue (starting with the genetic component) that experts at the University of Technology Sydney have developed, presenting their work in Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine (first author Yue (Eric) Yang). The system analyses a person’s DNA to identify genetic risk factors for stroke with greater accuracy, paving the way for risk assessments tailored to each individual, partly by combining this data with traditional risk factors.

According to Yang, this is a unique AI algorithm because “it not only identifies genetic variants linked to stroke, but also takes into account their location in the genome and possible interactions – as the researcher states in a note from the Australian university –”. For the record, the prototype was tested using genetic and health data from the UK Biobank database, comparing it with medical records from a large US database (All-of-Us). It proved to be more accurate than previous genetic risk assessment tools in distinguishing between people who had suffered a stroke and those who were healthy. In particular, the analysis identified 18 different genetic variants associated with ischaemic stroke. It was found that those with a higher genetic risk score were 22 per cent more likely to suffer a stroke than the control group. In particular, there appears to be a gene in the cerebral cortex that represents a key factor in susceptibility to ischaemic stroke. It is called EDEM2 and could provide a specific target for further biological research into the causes of stroke. For the record, the Australian experts used the same technology that underpins large-scale language models such as ChatGPT to train the model on thousands of genetic variants and identify links with ischaemic stroke.

We would like to reiterate this. Genetics is only one part of the risk profile. This is why the ability to combine a genetic score with clinical and lifestyle information – including known risk factors such as blood pressure, age, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes and cholesterol – could improve monitoring and prevention by designing a personalised pathway, and not just for young people. And this is precisely the aim of the research, with experts turning to AI to identify associations between genes and diseases and to develop personalised risk assessments for targeted prevention. The aim is therefore to develop a multimodal tool based on artificial intelligence capable of combining a genetic risk assessment with other types of data, including health and lifestyle questionnaires, scans and diagnostic images.

The future? As reported by Kairui Guo, who collaborated with the dedicated unit at Liverpool Hospital in Sydney on the analysis of genomic data and the application of artificial intelligence to the management of acute stroke, alongside Dennis Cordato, AI will help to understand the actual risk faced by the relatives of stroke patients, particularly those who suffer a stroke at a young age. “We have a proposal for a preventive clinical trial,” says Guo. “The aim is to recruit the first cohort of patients, sequence their genomes and analyse their risk of stroke. We are also interested in gender differences in stroke risk between men and women.”

“The Australian study is interesting, but it should be viewed with a sense of realism,” says Vincenzo Andreone, director of the Complex Operational Unit of Neurology and Stroke Unit at the Cardarelli Hospital in Naples. “The finding that those with the most unfavourable genetic profile have a 22 per cent higher risk of stroke is important but not groundbreaking. Even a few years ago, using much simpler tools, we were already seeing similar or even higher figures.” In short, clinical trials will allow us to better understand the model’s accuracy. But the real innovation lies in the method. And in the prospects opened up by the use of AI. “Artificial Intelligence does not merely add up ‘at-risk’ genes: it looks at how they interact with one another, a bit like a reader who understands a sentence not from the individual words but from their order,” concludes Andreone. “The EDEM2 gene, identified as a possible key player, is for now merely a lead to be investigated further. Of course, this research can be particularly useful for families in which a young person has suffered a stroke, to help identify which relatives need to be more vigilant. One thing, however, must be made clear: DNA matters, but blood pressure, smoking, weight, a healthy lifestyle and exercise matter more. And it is on these factors that we must take action every day.”

Notizie e approfondimenti sugli avvenimenti politici, economici e finanziari.
